title: Random Variable
body:
A random variable is **a function from outcomes to numbers.** Roll two dice and the outcome is an
ordered pair; the random variable $X = $ "the sum" maps it to $2$ through $12$. That is the whole
definition, and it is worth being precise about because "variable" is misleading: $X$ is neither
random nor a variable, it is a deterministic function whose input happens to be random.

The point of the move is that you can do arithmetic on numbers and not on outcomes. Once outcomes
become numbers you can average them, square them, add two of them together, and the entire rest of
[[STATISTICS]] follows.

Notation: capital $X$ for the variable, lowercase $x$ for a value it takes, so $P(X = x)$ reads
sensibly.

## Discrete versus continuous

| | Discrete | Continuous |
|---|---|---|
| Values | countable | an interval |
| Described by | mass function $p(x) = P(X=x)$ | [[Probability Density Function\|density]] $f(x)$ |
| Total is 1 | $\sum_x p(x) = 1$ | $\int f(x)\,dx = 1$ |
| Interval probability | sum the terms | $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ |
| $P(X = x)$ | can be positive | **always $0$** |

Same theory, sums replaced by [[Integral|integrals]]. That substitution is why [[CALCULUS 1]] is
the prerequisite for this course, and it is the only real difficulty in block 2.

## Expected value

$$
E[X] = \sum_x x\,p(x)
\qquad\qquad
E[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x f(x)\,dx
$$

The **long-run average** of $X$: the [[Mean]] promoted from a dataset to a distribution, and
literally a weighted mean with the probabilities as weights. $\mu$ and $E[X]$ are the same symbol
twice.

Two warnings. The expected value need not be a possible value ($E[\text{die}] = 3.5$), and it need
not exist at all for heavy-tailed distributions where the integral diverges.

**Expectation is linear, unconditionally:**

$$
E[aX + bY + c] = aE[X] + bE[Y] + c
$$

with no independence required anywhere. This is the single most useful identity in probability,
because it lets you decompose a horrible variable into a sum of easy indicator variables and add up
their expectations. The binomial mean $np$ is exactly that argument: $n$ Bernoulli indicators, each
with expectation $p$.

For a function of $X$, do **not** apply $g$ to the mean:

$$
E[g(X)] = \sum_x g(x)\,p(x) \neq g(E[X]) \quad\text{in general}
$$

$E[X^2] \neq (E[X])^2$, and the gap between them is precisely the variance. That inequality has a
name (Jensen's) and it is why [[Cross-Entropy]] and [[KL Divergence]] behave the way they do.

## Variance of a random variable

$$
\text{Var}(X) = E\big[(X - \mu)^2\big] = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2
$$

Same object as the [[Variance]] of a dataset, defined against a distribution instead of a sample.
The rules carry over unchanged: $\text{Var}(aX + b) = a^2\text{Var}(X)$, and
$\text{Var}(X + Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y)$ **only if $X$ and $Y$ are independent**.

Independence for variables means $P(X \leq x, Y \leq y) = P(X \leq x)P(Y \leq y)$ for all $x,y$, the
[[Conditional Probability]] condition applied to every pair of events. Independence implies
$E[XY] = E[X]E[Y]$; the converse is false, and that gap is why zero [[Correlation]] does not mean
independence.

## Why this note matters outside the course

Nearly everything in fourth-year computer science that looks like a formula is an expectation of a function of a
random variable:

- [[Shannon Entropy]] is $H(X) = -E[\log P(X)]$, written out as $-\sum P(x)\log P(x)$. It is an
  expected [[Information]] content, and Evan's note states it in exactly that form.
- [[Cross-Entropy]] takes the expectation under one distribution of the log of another
- A [[Loss Function]] is minimised in expectation over the data distribution, which is what
  "expected risk" means, and [[Gradient Descent]] estimates that expectation with a minibatch
- Average-case [[Time Complexity]] is $E[\text{steps}]$ over an input distribution

None of those parse without this note, which is why the syllabus calls it the foundation of the
information theory set.

## Related

- [[Probability Distribution]]: the standard families and what $E[X]$ and $\text{Var}(X)$ are for each
- [[Probability Density Function]]: the continuous machinery in full
- [[Sampling Distribution]]: $\bar{X}$ is itself a random variable, which is the idea block 3 turns on
- [[Mean]] and [[Variance]]: the sample versions of these two summaries
